In 1973, a study conducted in Greece by Stratigos evaluated the use of spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) for the treatment of gonorrhea in adult and adolescent males with genital infections. The outcomes assessed included microbiological cure, but no specific details on clinical cure or side effects were mentioned. 2. In 2002, a study in China by Tian investigated the efficacy of spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) and ceftriaxone (250 mg intramuscularly, single dose) in adults and adolescents aged 18–52 with genital, rectal, and pharyngeal gonorrhea. The study reported microbiological and clinical cure rates but did not provide detailed information on side effects. 3. In 1993 and 1984, studies conducted in the Philippines by Tupasi used the same data to evaluate spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) in women aged 13–30 with culture-positive gonorrhea involving the cervix and urethra. The outcomes included microbiological cure and side effects, but no further details were provided. 4. In 1974, a study in the United Kingdom by Willcox assessed spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) in adult and adolescent males with acute uncomplicated urethral gonorrhea. The study reported microbiological cure and side effects, but the inclusion and exclusion criteria were unclear. 5. In 1990, a Polish study by Wójtowicz (published in Polish) evaluated spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) in adults and adolescents with genital gonorrhea. The study reported microbiological cure rates but did not specify inclusion or exclusion criteria. 6. In 2000, a study in China by Zhou (published in Chinese) investigated spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) in adults and adolescents aged 18–52 with gonorrhea. Patients with allergies, pregnancy, breastfeeding, or significant cardiac, renal, or liver complications were excluded. The study assessed microbiological and clinical cure rates as well as side effects. 7. Randomized controlled trials analyzed the efficacy of gentamicin (5 mg/kg) versus ceftriaxone (500 mg intramuscularly) for microbiological cure at 7–14 days. Adverse events were also reported. Dual therapy regimens combining ceftriaxone or gentamicin with azithromycin were compared for microbiological cure and adverse events. 8. Ceftriaxone (250 mg intramuscularly, single dose) was evaluated in case series and comparative studies for microbiological cure by infection. Adverse events were also assessed. 9. Studies comparing ceftriaxone (500 mg intramuscularly, single dose) with azithromycin (1 g or 2 g) reported microbiological cure rates by person and infection, as well as adverse events. 10. Cefixime (400 mg or 800 mg) was evaluated for microbiological cure by person and infection. Adverse events were reported, but no additional details were provided. 11. Spectinomycin (2 g intramuscularly, single dose) was assessed for microbiological cure by person and adverse events in the treatment of gonorrhea. 12. Evidence from systematic reviews and WHO guidelines highlighted the effectiveness of dual therapy (e.g., ceftriaxone plus azithromycin) compared to monotherapy for treating Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). Cost-effectiveness and patient/provider acceptability were also analyzed. 13. Surveys and retrospective reviews in various countries (e.g., United States, United Kingdom, China, Netherlands) revealed variations in adherence to treatment guidelines, prescribing practices, and patient compliance. Factors influencing non-adherence included geographic location, healthcare setting, and lack of knowledge about national guidelines. 14. Cost-effectiveness studies suggested that dual therapy may be more cost-effective in the long term compared to monotherapy, particularly in the context of increasing antimicrobial resistance. However, the benefits of dual therapy may diminish if resistance to azithromycin is already prevalent. 15. Equity and feasibility studies addressed disparities in treatment access and the practicality of implementing different regimens. For example, single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone was preferred for its simplicity and patient compliance, but challenges in resource-limited settings were noted. 16. The Chinese National STD Treatment Guidelines align with WHO recommendations for single therapy (e.g., ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly or spectinomycin 2 g intramuscularly, single dose) but do not recommend dual therapy with azithromycin. Non-adherence to guidelines was associated with factors such as working in northern China, general hospitals, and lack of knowledge about recommended regimens. 17. Studies on acceptability indicated that both patients and providers preferred single-dose intramuscular regimens over multiple oral doses due to better compliance. However, opinions on culture-based oral therapy versus blind intramuscular therapy were mixed. 18. Cost analyses compared targeted ciprofloxacin therapy with dual therapy (ceftriaxone plus azithromycin) in different scenarios, considering factors such as testing frequency and resistance prevalence. Dual therapy was found to be cost-effective only under specific conditions. 19. Retrospective reviews in emergency departments and other clinical settings highlighted the variability in treatment practices, with some patients receiving non-guideline-compliant regimens. However, most regimens included at least one recommended agent. 20. Surveys of general practitioners revealed diverse opinions on the feasibility and acceptability of different treatment regimens, with some resistance to intramuscular administration of ceftriaxone due to perceived inconvenience.
